title: Money Columns
context: Grade 3, the fourth working topic of the money chapter. An adult sees a column sum, which a worksheet shows well. What is being settled is that the dot, not the right edge, is what the numbers line up on, that a hundred paise are exactly one rupee and cross from the paise column to the rupees column as a single one, and that borrowing a rupee gives the paise a hundred, not ten. A child who lines the amounts up on the right will add rupees to paise with great confidence, and a child who borrows ten paise will take away the wrong amount.

writeup.why: Set two amounts one under the other with the dots in a line, add them by carrying one rupee for a hundred paise, subtract them by borrowing one rupee as a hundred paise, and turn a money story into one of the two sums.
writeup.look: A board ruled into a deep blue Rupees column and a vermilion Paise column, an amber shelf of price tags, a green answer row, the Carry, Borrow and Plain columns buttons, and the number pad down the right of the canvas.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Money Columns' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at x 64, y 108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: how many amounts have been worked out. It is never a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at x 64, y 202. A plain wall fills the working area. The board stands at x 100, y 226, 640 by 450, a cream card with a thin near-black outline. A Rupees heading in deep blue stands over its left part and a Paise heading in vermilion over its right part, at y 238. A thin vertical dot line at x 520 runs the height of the board and every dot stands on it. The first amount is written at y 306 and the second at y 396, each digit in its own square cell 56 across, the rupees cells in deep blue and the paise cells in vermilion, with the operation sign alone at x 126, y 396 in near-black. A rule runs under the second row at y 462, and the answer row stands under it at y 480 in a thick green outline. A round carry cell, 44 across, sits above the Rupees column at x 380, y 262, and a borrow strip, 300 by 36, above the first row at x 190, y 268. The amber price tags hang on a shelf at x 790, y 226, 300 by 230, one tag for each amount. The Carry button stands at x 100, y 692, 160 by 56, the Borrow button at x 280, y 692, 160 by 56, the Show tags button at x 460, y 692, 190 by 56 and the Plain columns button at x 670, y 692, 220 by 56, each labelled in words. In a story the board sits in a small scene drawn behind it: a school fair stall, a shop counter, a purse or a money box, with a bill slip and a plain flat note or two beside it. In the Plain columns view the same board is drawn alone with no scene. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at x 1186, y 250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at x 1170, y 368 (388 by 363). The pad is ten number keys, a dot key and a clear key, for typing the rupees, the dot and the paise of the answer into the answer slot. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Real objects keep their own natural colours. The whole rupees of an amount are deep blue and the paise are vermilion everywhere, in a column heading, a tag and a label. The value written on one note or coin, and the price of one thing, is amber. How many notes, coins or things there are is sky blue. A total, a change, a converted amount and the answer are green. A note is a plain flat rectangle in its own colour and a coin a plain round disc, each with its value in large near-black type, so a value is read from the number and never from the colour. Anything dimmed fades to half strength rather than turning grey, and chrome never borrows one of the five. Each reading survives with the colour taken away, because an amount is told by its written label before it is told by its colour.
writeup.finish: The board shows the last sum with its carry or its borrow, and the answer row reads the amount in green.

phases.win: the dots fall into one line, the two headings light in their own colours, and a whole amount shows its two zeros
phases.does: drags each part of both amounts into its column, checks that the dots line up, and writes two zeros after a whole amount
phases.goal: rupees stand under rupees, paise under paise, the dots make one straight line, and a whole number of rupees takes two zeros
phases.says: Which column does each part belong in? Do the dots stand in one straight line?
phases.check: Away from the screen: write Rs 8 and Rs 19.60 one under the other. What do you write after the dot of Rs 8?
phases.feels: the digits sliding into their columns until every dot stands on the same line
phases.hands: Give each pair two paper price tags and a sheet ruled into a Rupees column and a Paise column, and ask them to write the rupees under the rupees and the paise under the paise.
phases.tries: First rung: say which part of the amount is the rupees. Second rung: slide the digits until the dots touch the dot line. Third rung: the same task with the whole amount set first, before the second amount returns.

wrong.why: whole numbers are lined up on the right, so the same habit is brought to money
wrong.move: lines the amounts up on the right edge so the paise sit under the rupees
wrong.screen: the Rupees and Paise headings stay lit, the dot line is drawn through the board, and the digits are slid back until every dot stands on it

wrong.why: an amount with no paise looks complete without them
wrong.move: leaves out the zeros of a whole amount, so the paise column is empty
wrong.screen: the paise cells of that amount blink once and two zeros are written in, so the whole amount is read as rupees and no paise

phases.screen: the empty board at a fair stall with two price tags waiting on the shelf and the dot line drawn between the columns
phases.soWhat: rupees go under rupees, paise go under paise, and the dots stand in one straight line
phases.concept: Rupees under rupees, paise under paise

phases.win: a bundle of a hundred paise slides across and lands as one rupee, and the answer row lights green
phases.does: adds the paise, presses Carry when they reach a hundred, adds the rupees with the carried one, and types the answer
phases.goal: the paise are added first, and a hundred paise or more send one rupee across to the rupees column
phases.says: Add the paise first. Do they make a hundred or more?
phases.check: Away from the screen: 70 paise plus 60 paise. How many paise are left under Paise, and how many rupees do you carry?
phases.feels: a hundred paise sliding across the board and landing as a single rupee
phases.hands: Add the paise first on a sheet ruled into two columns, and when they make a hundred or more, trade a hundred paise for a Rs 1 coin and put the coin in the rupees column.
phases.tries: First rung: add only the paise and say the total. Second rung: say how many hundreds are in the total. Third rung: the same task with the paise adding to just over a hundred, before bigger totals return.

wrong.why: the paise were added correctly, but the hundred is left where it was made
wrong.move: writes all the paise of the sum under Paise, so the paise column has three digits
wrong.screen: the Paise column holds only two cells, so the extra hundred paise rise out of it as a bundle and slide over to the carry cell as one rupee

wrong.why: the carry is written small and is easy to pass over
wrong.move: adds the rupees and forgets the carried rupee
wrong.screen: the carry cell glows deep blue until it is added, and the rupees are counted again with the carried one included

phases.screen: the board with two amounts set, a plus sign at the left of the second row, and a round carry cell above the rupees
phases.soWhat: add the paise first, and carry one rupee to the rupees for every hundred paise
phases.concept: Adding: a hundred paise carry one rupee

phases.win: one rupee breaks into a hundred paise, the rupees drop by one, and the answer row lights green
phases.does: looks at the paise, presses Borrow when they are too few, takes away the paise and then the rupees, and types the answer
phases.goal: the smaller amount goes below the bigger, and when the top paise are too few one rupee breaks into a hundred paise
phases.says: Look at the top paise. Are there enough to take away?
phases.check: Away from the screen: you borrow Rs 1 and the top paise were 20. How many paise are there now, and what happened to the rupees?
phases.feels: one rupee breaking into a hundred paise and the rupees column dropping by one
phases.hands: Hold a Rs 1 coin over the rupees column, and when the top paise are too few, swap it for a hundred paise and put the paise in the paise column.
phases.tries: First rung: compare the top paise with the paise to take away. Second rung: press Borrow and say how many paise there are now. Third rung: the same task with a whole amount on top, before the paise appear on top.

wrong.why: taking the smaller digit from the bigger always works in a single column
wrong.move: takes the smaller paise from the bigger paise the wrong way round
wrong.screen: the paise are shown in a row with the top amount first, the borrow strip opens, and the paise to take away are counted from the top amount only

wrong.why: borrowing ten is the habit from whole numbers, where the next place is worth ten
wrong.move: borrows ten paise instead of a hundred
wrong.screen: the borrowed rupee breaks into a hundred small paise, counted in tens across the cells, so ten tens fill the paise column

phases.screen: the board with a bigger amount above a smaller one, a minus sign at the left, and a borrow strip above the top row
phases.soWhat: borrow one rupee, count it as a hundred paise, take the paise, and then take the rupees
phases.concept: Subtracting: one rupee borrowed is a hundred paise

phases.win: the amounts settle into the columns, the answer lights green, and the bill and the note show the same amounts
phases.does: reads the story, chooses to add or to subtract, sets the amounts in columns, works them and types the answer
phases.goal: a story that puts money together is added, and a story about what is left, the change or how much more is subtracted
phases.says: Read the story. Do we put money together or take money away?
phases.check: Away from the screen: Rs 50 is in a purse and Rs 18 is spent. Do you add or take away, and what is left?
phases.feels: the story settling into the columns and the right sign taking its place
phases.hands: Read a short story aloud and ask whether the money is put together or taken away, and then act it out with dummy notes and coins on the counter.
phases.tries: First rung: say in your own words what the story asks. Second rung: say whether the money is put together or taken away. Third rung: the same story with one amount only, before the second amount returns.

wrong.why: two amounts are named and adding is the first thing that comes to mind
wrong.move: adds the note and the bill to find the change
wrong.screen: the note and the bill are laid side by side on the counter, the bill is taken from the note, and the change is what is left

wrong.why: the story names a purse and a change, so taking away seems right
wrong.move: subtracts the two prices when the story asks how much in all
wrong.screen: the two prices slide together onto one bill slip and the board switches to an adding sum, with the plus sign at the left

phases.screen: a shop counter with a bill, a note and a purse beside the board, and a short money story written above it
phases.soWhat: add to find how much in all, and subtract to find how much is left, the change or how much more
phases.concept: Money problems: how much in all, how much left, how much change

writeup.delight: On the second phase, as the paise are added, the bundle of a hundred paise slides across the board so slowly that it seems to hesitate, and when it lands in the carry cell it turns into a single rupee coin and the answer row lights green. On the third phase, one rupee coin breaks into a hundred small paise that rain softly into the paise cells.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing yet typed. On the first phase the empty board stands at a fair stall with the dot line drawn between the two columns and two amber price tags on the shelf. On the second a plus sign stands at the left of the second row with both amounts already set, the paise column lit first and a round carry cell empty above the rupees. On the third a minus sign stands at the left, the bigger amount is above the smaller, and a borrow strip waits above the top row. On the fourth a shop counter holds a bill, a note and a purse beside the board, with a short money story above it. One thing moves, once: the dot line gives one slow pulse while the voice speaks its opening line, and a finger on a digit is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any two amounts on the board, with the carry and borrow buttons, the tags shelf and the plain columns view all open. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on setting amounts in columns, adding with a carry, subtracting with a borrow and money stories, each in a small real scene.
voiceLines: A board with two columns, and two price tags waiting to be set.
Which column does each part belong in? Do the dots stand in one straight line?
Add the paise first. Do they make a hundred or more?
Look at the top paise. Are there enough to take away?
Read the story. Do we put money together or take money away?
A new sum. Which part will you work first?
Free play. Set any two amounts and work them as you like.
Look at the dots again. Do the rupees and the paise stand in their own columns?

observations.why: the dot is the mark that divides every amount into rupees and paise, so it is what the amounts line up on.
observations.soWhat: rupees go under rupees, paise go under paise, and the dots make one straight line.
observations.observe: When the amounts were set one under the other, the dots stood in one straight line only when the rupees were under the rupees and the paise under the paise.

observations.why: a hundred paise are one rupee, so every full hundred of paise moves across as a single one.
observations.soWhat: add the paise first, write the paise that are left, and carry one rupee for each hundred.
observations.observe: When the paise made a hundred or more, a bundle of a hundred paise slid over to the rupees column and landed as exactly one rupee.

observations.why: one rupee is worth a hundred paise, so what leaves the rupees arrives in the paise as a hundred.
observations.soWhat: borrow one rupee, count it as a hundred paise, take the paise and then the rupees.
observations.observe: When the top paise were too few, one rupee broke into a hundred paise and the rupees column dropped by exactly one.

observations.why: the same board answers how much in all, how much is left and how much change, depending on what the story asks.
observations.soWhat: add to find how much in all, and take away to find how much is left, the change or how much more.
observations.observe: A story that put money together was set as an adding sum, and a story about what was left or the change was set as a taking away sum.

source_tool.description: A cream board stands at the left of the working area, ruled into a Rupees column headed in deep blue and a Paise column headed in vermilion, with one thin vertical line between them that carries every dot. Two amounts are written one under the other, each digit in its own cell, with the operation sign alone at the far left of the second row, a rule under it and a green answer row below. A small round carry cell sits above the Rupees column and a borrow strip above the first row. A shelf at the right holds amber price tags, and a Show tags button slides the amounts onto it as they are named. A Carry button gathers a hundred paise into a bundle that slides across to the Rupees column, and a Borrow button breaks one rupee into a hundred paise. In the stories the board sits in a small scene, a school fair stall, a shop counter, a purse or a money box, with a bill and a note beside it. The number pad types the answer, and a dot key and a clear key sit beside the ten digits. The running count at the top left of the canvas says how many amounts have been worked out. A Plain columns button redraws the same board with no scene.
source_tool.art_direction: A fair stall and shop counter / Picture book

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight
zones.title: the phase title beside that dot, on the same single header line
zones.voice: the caption at the far left of the footer, its speaking dot beside it
zones.chrome: again, sound and restart, as round controls at the far right of the header

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets, big enough for a small finger. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Money is drawn as plain flat shapes: a note is a rectangle in its own colour and a coin a round disc, each with its value in large near-black type. There is no portrait, no emblem, no serial number and no small print on any note or coin, because a child reads the value from the number. The notes are Rs 500, Rs 200, Rs 100, Rs 50, Rs 20 and Rs 10, and the coins Rs 20, Rs 10, Rs 5, Rs 2 and Rs 1. A note is always longer than it is tall and a coin is always round.

Real everyday things hold the money and the prices: a purse, a money box, a shop shelf with a price tag on each thing, a bill on a counter, a school fair stall. The object is the thing the child counts, pays or reads, and a bare column of figures appears only as a second view the child can switch to.

An amount is always written Rs 25.50: Rs, then the rupees, then a dot, then exactly two digits of paise. Rs 5 and 5 paise is Rs 5.05, and a single digit of paise after the dot is never written. A whole number of rupees may be written without the dot, as Rs 36, or with two zeros, as Rs 36.00.

In a column sum the dots stand in one straight line, rupees to the left of it and paise to the right, with a heading Rupees over one part and Paise over the other. A carry or a borrow of one rupee is written small above the rupees column and its hundred paise above the paise column.
A price is a tag on the thing it belongs to. A bill is a table of the thing, how many, the price of one and the cost, with a rule under the last line and the total below.
Anything the stage asks to be counted is at most thirty things, separated and large enough to count at a glance.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a note, a coin, an amount or a number the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. Real objects keep their own natural colours: a note keeps its own colour, a coin its own metal, a purse its own leather. The whole rupees of an amount are deep blue and the paise are vermilion everywhere, in a column heading, a tag, a label and a typed answer, because the dot between them is the one mark that tells a child which part is which. The value written on one note or coin, and the price of one thing, is amber. How many notes, coins or things there are is sky blue. A total, a change, a converted amount and the answer are green. Those five are the same five in every tool and every picture of this chapter. Each role is named in writing first, with the words Rupees, Paise, Value, How many and Answer, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.
voice.where: The caption line sits at the far left of the footer with a small dot beside it that glows while the voice is talking. An again control repeats the last line.
voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: Look at the dots again. Do the rupees and the paise stand in their own columns?
voice.onNext: A new sum. Which part will you work first?
voice.opening: A board with two columns, and two price tags waiting to be set.
voice.onFinish: You kept the dots in one line and worked the paise first.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Set any two amounts and work them as you like.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.
voice.voicePreference: an English voice, female where one is offered

phase_map.concept: Rupees under rupees, paise under paise
Adding: a hundred paise carry one rupee
Subtracting: one rupee borrowed is a hundred paise
Money problems: how much in all, how much left, how much change

placement.where: After each child has set out two prices from paper price tags on a sheet ruled into a Rupees column and a Paise column and worked a pair by hand, and before any column sum is written on the board. The tool is what lets a hundred paise gather and cross to the rupees as one rupee, and one rupee break into a hundred paise, which a worksheet can only say.

answer_key.rule: To add or subtract money, set the amounts one under the other so that rupees stand under rupees, paise under paise and the dots make one straight line. If an amount has no paise, write two zeros after the dot. To add, add the paise first. If they make 100 paise or more, write the paise over 100 and carry 1 rupee to the rupees column, then add the rupees. To subtract, put the smaller amount below the bigger one and take the paise first. If the top paise are too few, borrow 1 rupee from the rupees and count it as 100 paise, then take the rupees. Adding finds how much in all. Subtracting finds how much is left, the change or how much more.
answer_key.wrong: The board is shown again with the two amounts in their columns and the dots in a line, and the paise worked first with the carry or the borrow lit in turn. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: Rs 13.40 is 13 rupees and 40 paise. Rs 7.85 is 7 rupees and 85 paise.
Put the rupees under the rupees and the paise under the paise.
The 7 is the ones place of the rupees, so it sits under the 3 of 13.
The two dots stand in one straight line, and the 40 sits above the 85.
items.answer: The 7 goes under the 3 of 13, in the Rupees column. The dots make one straight line.
items.question: A fair stall shows two prices, Rs 13.40 and Rs 7.85. Set them one under the other in a Rupees column and a Paise column. Where does the 7 go, and where do the dots go?
items.checkpoint: Rupees go under rupees and paise go under paise, so the dots make one straight line.
items.misconception: Lining the numbers up on the right edge, so the 85 paise sit under the 3 rupees.

steps: Add the paise first: 30 paise plus 85 paise is 115 paise.
115 paise is Rs 1 and 15 paise. Write 15 under Paise and carry Rs 1 to the rupees.
Add the rupees: Rs 15 plus Rs 22 is Rs 37, and Rs 37 plus Rs 1 is Rs 38.
Put the dot in the answer: Rs 15.30 plus Rs 22.85 is Rs 38.15.
items.question: At a pet shop, a fish bowl costs Rs 15.30 and fish food costs Rs 22.85. How much do they cost in all?
items.checkpoint: When the paise make 100 or more, write the extra paise and carry 1 rupee.
items.misconception: Writing 115 under Paise, so the answer has three digits of paise.

steps: Put the smaller amount below the bigger one. Take the paise first.
The top paise are 10. We cannot take 35 paise from 10 paise, so borrow Rs 1.
Rs 1 is 100 paise. 100 paise plus 10 paise is 110 paise, and 110 paise minus 35 paise is 75 paise.
The rupees fall from 80 to 79. Rs 79 minus Rs 41 is Rs 38, so Rs 80.10 minus Rs 41.35 is Rs 38.75.
items.question: A pencil box costs Rs 80.10 and a ruler costs Rs 41.35. How much more does the pencil box cost?
items.checkpoint: When the top paise are too few, borrow 1 rupee and count it as 100 paise.
items.misconception: Taking the smaller paise from the bigger paise the wrong way round, 35 minus 10.

steps: Putting money together means adding. Rs 46.50 plus Rs 19.25 is Rs 65.75.
Change means taking the bill from the note. Write the note as Rs 100.00.
She spends Rs 65.75 and gets Rs 34.25 back.
items.answer: She spends Rs 65.75 and gets Rs 34.25 change.
items.question: A child buys a notebook for Rs 46.50 and a pen for Rs 19.25. She pays with a Rs 100 note. How much does she spend in all, and how much change does she get?
items.checkpoint: Add to find how much in all, and subtract the bill from the note to find the change.
items.misconception: Adding the note and the bill instead of taking the bill from the note.

learn.shape: Worked items, shown solved, mandatory before practice unlocks.
learn.selection: Fixed order, walking the phases from the first to the last.
learn.content_criterion: One per phase, so Learn walks the whole topic and stops.

items.question: A fair stall sells a balloon for Rs 9 and a mask for Rs 23.45. Write both prices in columns. What goes under Paise for the balloon?
items.final_answer: Two zeros, 00. The balloon is Rs 9.00, with its dot in line with the dot of Rs 23.45

items.question: A bus ticket costs Rs 31.20 and a train ticket costs Rs 14.35. How much do the two tickets cost together?
A scarf costs Rs 38.90 and a cap costs Rs 13.50. Take Rs 13.50 from Rs 38.90 in columns. Do you need to borrow?
items.final_answer: No. The answer is Rs 25.40, because 90 paise is more than 50 paise

items.question: A girl has Rs 86.50 in her purse. She buys a puzzle for Rs 32.25. How much money is left?
Write Rs 6.40 and Rs 126.05 in columns. How many digits does each amount have in the Rupees column, and where does the 6 of Rs 6.40 stand?
items.final_answer: Rs 126.05 has three digits and Rs 6.40 has one. The 6 stands under the last digit of 126, so the dots line up

items.question: Two shop bills come to Rs 57.90 and Rs 26.65. What is the total of the two bills?
items.final_answer: Rs 84.55, because 90 paise and 65 paise make more than a hundred, so write 55 and carry Rs 1

items.question: A toy car costs Rs 50. A toy bus costs Rs 17.60. How much more does the car cost? Write Rs 50 with two zeros after the dot first.
items.final_answer: Rs 32.40. Rs 50.00 has no paise to take 60 from, so borrow Rs 1: 100 paise minus 60 paise is 40 paise, and Rs 49 minus Rs 17 is Rs 32

items.question: A child pays with a Rs 200 note for a bag at Rs 98.75 and a water bottle at Rs 47.50. How much is the bill, and how much change does the child get?
items.final_answer: The bill is Rs 146.25 and the change is Rs 53.75

practice.selection: Fixed order, easy first, and every phase represented.
practice.interaction_rules: Answered on the tool itself. A wrong answer returns the question with a hint; nothing is marked and retries are unlimited.

student_controls.effect: take the digits of an amount, so each stands in its own column
gathers a hundred paise into a bundle that slides to the Rupees column as one rupee
breaks one rupee into a hundred paise and lowers the rupees by one
slides each amount onto an amber price tag on the shelf
redraws the same board with no scene
types the rupees and the paise of the answer, with a dot key and a clear key

teaching_notes: Give each pair two paper price tags and a sheet ruled into a Rupees column and a Paise column before the tool opens, and ask them to set the tags one under the other and say what is under what. Always ask where the dots are before any digit is added, and have the paise worked first with a finger on the Paise column. Wait for a child to say that a hundred paise are one rupee, rather than saying it for them. Say carry when a hundred paise go over to the rupees and borrow when a rupee comes over to the paise, every time. If a child lines the numbers up on the right edge, ask which part of each amount is the rupees. Use fresh amounts: the printed sums are the child's to set out and work.
generation_prompt: Build a money column tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage. A cream board stands at the left of the working area, ruled into a Rupees column headed in deep blue and a Paise column headed in vermilion, with one thin vertical line between them that carries every dot. Two amounts are written one under the other, each digit in its own cell, with the operation sign alone at the far left of the second row, a rule under it and a green answer row. A round carry cell sits above the Rupees column and a borrow strip above the first row. A Carry button gathers a hundred paise into a bundle that slides across to the Rupees column, and a Borrow button breaks one rupee into a hundred paise. A shelf of amber price tags stands at the right. Each task sits in a small scene, a school fair stall, a shop counter, a purse or a money box. Notes are plain flat rectangles and coins plain flat discs with only their value on them, and no rupee sign is drawn: an amount is written Rs 25.50. The number pad types the answer, with a dot key and a clear key. The running count at the top left of the canvas is the number of amounts worked out. No people, hands or faces. Pointer events only, no assets, no network. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right. No sidebar, and no score box anywhere. One phase, one mount: build the phase the host passes and nothing else (tool_config.phase_mount). The first frame comes from writeup.opening. Each phase comes from writeup.phases, with its screen, action, reward and spoken line; its tries field is the hint ladder and its wrong list is what the stage does about a wrong answer, redrawn in steps on the working area with nothing marked and nothing reset. The one surprise is writeup.delight. The look and the sounds come from tool_config.style, voice and audio.
instructions_for_student: Set the two amounts in the columns. Make the dots stand in one straight line. Work the paise first. Carry or borrow one rupee when you need to.
